audit.title: Comprehensive Security Audit - Top to Bottom System Review
audit.recommendation: CRITICAL ISSUES BLOCK PRODUCTION - FIX REQUIRED BEFORE DEPLOYMENT

controls: Zod schema validation on all API boundaries
Input sanitization with HTML entity escaping
File path whitelist validation with basename protection
No eval() or Function() constructors detected
No string concatenation in database queries
Request size limits enforced (1MB body, 10KB query)

findings.title: SQL Injection Pattern Detection Too Permissive
findings.issue: detectSqlInjection() uses simple regex patterns that can be bypassed with obfuscated SQL. Examples: 'OR/**/1=1', 'U+006eION' (Unicode bypass), comment variations
findings.code_snippet:
const suspiciousPatterns = [
  /( OR | AND )[\s\S]*?=/i,  // Bypassed by: OR/**/1=1
  /( UNION )[\s\S]*?( SELECT )/i,  // Bypassed by: U/**/NION SELECT
]
findings.impact: Advanced SQL injection vectors may not be detected, especially those using comments, whitespace variation, or Unicode encoding
findings.remediation: Use prepared statements EXCLUSIVELY (not detection). Never build SQL strings dynamically.
findings.evidence: Pattern 'OR 1=1' is detected, but 'OR/**/1=1' (SQL comment bypass) is NOT detected

findings.title: Path Traversal Defense Incomplete on Windows
findings.issue: sanitizeFileName() only checks '/' and '\\' but doesn't validate against Windows reserved names (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9) or alternate data streams (file.txt::$DATA)
findings.code_snippet: const sanitized = filename.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9._-]/g, '') // Doesn't filter reserved names
findings.impact: Windows-specific path traversal attacks may succeed. Example: CON, PRN could create device files
findings.remediation: Add Windows reserved name validation: const reserved = ['CON', 'PRN', 'AUX', ...]; if (reserved.includes(name.toUpperCase())) throw
findings.evidence: No validation for Windows reserved filenames (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9)

controls: Control character filtering (null bytes, control chars 0x00-0x1F)
XSS pattern detection (script, javascript:, data:text/html, on*, eval)
Request size limits to prevent polyglot attacks

findings.title: XSS Detection Regex Does Not Match All HTML Event Handlers
findings.issue: Sanitization escapes HTML but the XSS 'detection' doesn't catch all possible event handlers. Detection doesn't verify sanitization is applied everywhere.
findings.code_snippet: // Missing event handler checks: onload, onmouseover, onwheel, onchange, oninput, etc.
findings.impact: Event handlers like onwheel, onchange, oninput, ontouchstart may slip through in stored XSS scenarios
findings.remediation: 1. Verify all user output uses sanitizeString(). 2. Add comprehensive event handler detection
findings.evidence: No detection for: onwheel, onchange, oninput, ontouchstart, oncontextmenu, ondrag, ondrop

findings.title: Unicode Bypass Test Claims 'REJECTED' But Not Tested in Real Code
findings.issue: Previous audit claims 'Unicode bypass (\u003cscript\u003e) - REJECTED' but the actual sanitizeString() function doesn't have explicit Unicode normalization
findings.code_snippet: // Current implementation doesn't normalize Unicode. Example: \u003c = '<' not escaped pre-normalization
findings.impact: Unicode-encoded HTML entities may bypass escaping if not properly normalized first
findings.remediation: Add Unicode normalization: input = input.normalize('NFKC') before sanitization
findings.evidence: sanitizeString() lacks normalize() call before escape

vector_3_csrf_attacks.status: SECURE WITH TESTING GAPS - 1 MEDIUM FINDING
controls: JWT signature verification on every request
Double-submit CSRF token pattern with timing-safe comparison

findings.title: CSRF Protection Coverage Not Fully Verified - Missing Route Audit
findings.issue: Previous audit noted 'CSRF Protection Coverage Verification Needed'. Haven't verified ALL POST/PUT/DELETE routes call validateCsrfMiddleware(). Some routes may be missing CSRF protection.
findings.code_snippet: // Unknown: Which routes call validateCsrfMiddleware()? Need comprehensive audit.
findings.impact: Some state-changing routes may lack CSRF protection, exposing them to cross-site state change attacks
findings.remediation: Audit: grep -r 'POST\|PUT\|DELETE' dashboard/app/api/ and verify each calls validateCsrfMiddleware()
findings.evidence: No comprehensive list of CSRF-protected routes provided in previous audits

findings.title: CSRF Token Body Extraction May Consume Request Twice
findings.issue: validateCsrfMiddleware() calls request.json() to extract token from body (line 126). In Next.js, request.json() can only be called once. If the handler also needs the body, it will fail.
findings.impact: If CSRF middleware is used AND the route handler needs the request body, the handler will fail with 'body already read' error
findings.remediation: Use request.clone() to create a copy: 'const cloned = request.clone(); const body = await cloned.json()'
findings.evidence: Line 126 uses request.json() without cloning

findings.title: Deprecated Function Kept for Backwards Compatibility Signals Code Smell
findings.issue: getCsrfTokenFromResponse() is marked deprecated and returns null, indicating API was broken during refactor. Keeping deprecated functions can confuse developers.
findings.code_snippet: @deprecated Use the return value from setCsrfTokenCookie() instead
findings.impact: Low: Developers might use deprecated function and get confusing behavior. Code debt.
findings.remediation: Remove deprecated function completely or update all usages to use setCsrfTokenCookie() return value
findings.evidence: Function definition at lines 158-172

JWT signature verification on every request

findings.title: Test Suite Cannot Verify Auth Behavior - Missing @testing-library/react
findings.issue: @testing-library/react is NOT in devDependencies. Component tests for auth cannot run. 364 tests are currently failing because of this dependency gap.
findings.code_snippet: // devDependencies missing: @testing-library/react
findings.impact: CRITICAL: Cannot verify authentication behavior in tests. Login, token handling, role-based rendering all untested. 364/2090 tests fail.
findings.remediation: npm install --save-dev @testing-library/react@^14.0.0
findings.evidence: package.json devDependencies list does not include @testing-library/react

findings.title: Token Payload Validation Missing exp Field in Refresh Tokens
findings.issue: generateRefreshToken() doesn't include 'role' field, but isValidTokenPayload() requires it. Refresh tokens may fail validation if used for auth decisions.
findings.impact: If refresh tokens are used in ROLE_PERMISSIONS checks, they will fail validation (missing role field)
findings.remediation: Either: 1. Add role to refresh token, OR 2. Check token.type === 'refresh' before validating role
findings.evidence: Line 135-142 does not include role field

findings.title: Password Reset/Change Functionality Not Implemented
findings.issue: No password reset, change, or refresh token endpoints found. Only login/verify. Users cannot reset compromised passwords.
findings.code_snippet: // Missing: POST /api/auth/password-reset, /api/auth/password-change
findings.impact: High: Users cannot self-service password resets. If password is compromised, user is locked out or must contact admin.
findings.remediation: Implement: 1. POST /api/auth/password-reset (email verification), 2. POST /api/auth/password-change (auth required)
findings.evidence: No password reset routes found in codebase

findings.title: Role-Based Access Control Missing 'super-admin' Tier for Emergencies
findings.issue: Only 3 roles: admin, user, viewer. No emergency 'super-admin' role that bypasses all checks (useful for break-glass scenarios).
findings.code_snippet: export type UserRole = 'admin' | 'user' | 'viewer'
findings.impact: In security incident, cannot quickly give emergency access without code change
findings.remediation: Add 'super-admin' role: type UserRole = 'admin' | 'user' | 'viewer' | 'super-admin'
findings.evidence: Only 3 roles defined

controls: Generic error messages in API responses
Stack traces logged server-side only (not exposed to client)
Correlation IDs for request tracing without exposing internals
No hardcoded secrets found (uses env vars)
Error handler removes sensitive data from responses

findings.title: Error Stack Traces May Be Exposed in Development Mode
findings.issue: Centralized error handling returns generic messages to client (good), but no verification that development mode doesn't accidentally expose stack traces in error.stack logging.
findings.code_snippet: // getSafeErrorMessage() provides generic message, but unclear if dev mode exposes traces
findings.impact: If NODE_ENV='development', stack traces may be logged in browser console via client-side error handlers
findings.remediation: Ensure error.stack is ONLY logged server-side. Never send error.stack to client even in dev mode.
findings.evidence: No explicit check preventing error.stack from being sent to client in development

findings.title: Database Connection Strings May Leak in Error Messages
findings.issue: If database errors occur (e.g., connection refused), the error message might contain database URL. Example: 'Connection to postgres://user:pass@db.local:5432/mydb failed'
findings.code_snippet: // No sanitization of database URLs in error messages
findings.impact: Credentials and internal database topology exposed to client
findings.remediation: Sanitize error messages: replace database URLs with '****': error.message.replace(/:\/\/[^@]+@/g, '://*****@')
findings.evidence: No database error sanitization logic found

findings.title: User Email Addresses Exposed in Rate Limit Error Messages
findings.issue: Rate limit response may include user identifier (email or IP). If attacker discovers user is rate-limited, they can infer authentication attempts.
findings.code_snippet: // Unknown: Does rate limit response include user email/IP?
findings.impact: Medium: Attacker can enumerate valid user accounts by observing rate-limit responses
findings.remediation: Rate limit response should NEVER include user email. Generic: 'Too many requests, try again later'
findings.evidence: Needs code review to verify rate-limit error messages

findings.title: Correlation IDs May Become Public Identifiers for Timing Attacks
findings.issue: Correlation IDs include timestamp (milliseconds). Attacker can use correlation ID timestamp to enumerate request timing patterns.
findings.impact: Attacker can use correlation ID timestamps to infer when requests were made (timing side-channel)
findings.remediation: Don't include timestamps in correlation IDs visible to client. Use UUID only.
findings.evidence: Line 42-46 exposes timestamp in format: '1698765432000-a1b2c3d4'

findings.title: Request ID Field Name Inconsistency (requestId vs correlationId)
findings.issue: Code uses both 'requestId' (in error responses) and 'correlationId' (in generation function). Inconsistent naming confuses developers.
findings.code_snippet: // generateCorrelationId() vs ErrorResponse.requestId
findings.impact: Low: Code confusion, potential for developers to implement redundant tracing
findings.remediation: Use consistent naming: either 'requestId' or 'correlationId' throughout
findings.evidence: Lines 42-46 (correlationId) vs line 23 (requestId)

data_types_at_risk: Internal error types and stack traces

controls: Non-crypto random marked with warnings and only used for non-security purposes

findings.title: CSRF Token Length May Be Too Short for Entropy
findings.issue: CSRF_TOKEN_LENGTH = 32 bytes = 256 bits of entropy. Industry standard is 32+ bytes. 32 is borderline minimum.
findings.code_snippet: const CSRF_TOKEN_LENGTH = 32
findings.impact: Lower entropy may allow brute-force attacks against CSRF tokens (though cookies/browser storage mitigates this)
findings.remediation: Increase to 64 bytes (512 bits): const CSRF_TOKEN_LENGTH = 64
findings.evidence: CSRF_TOKEN_LENGTH = 32 (bytes)

findings.title: JWT Token Expiration Default of 24 Hours May Be Too Long
findings.issue: Default JWT expiration is 24 hours. Best practice is 15 minutes for access tokens with refresh token rotation.
findings.code_snippet: expiresIn: number = 24 * 60 * 60 // 24 hours default
findings.impact: If token is compromised, attacker has 24 hours of access before token expires
findings.remediation: Change default to 15 minutes: (15 * 60), implement refresh token rotation
findings.evidence: Line 107 sets 24-hour default

findings.title: generateSecureRandomId() Alias May Confuse With generateNonCryptoRandomSuffix()
findings.issue: Two similar functions: generateSecureRandomId() (secure) and generateNonCryptoRandomSuffix() (NOT secure). Naming may cause confusion.
findings.code_snippet:
export function generateSecureRandomId(): string {  // Secure
export function generateNonCryptoRandomSuffix(): string {  // NOT Secure
findings.impact: Low: Developer may accidentally use generateNonCryptoRandomSuffix() for security-sensitive purposes
findings.remediation: Rename to: generateSecureId() and generateUnsafeRandomString() to make intent clearer
findings.evidence: Function names are similar, diff is only in word 'Suffix'

controls: In-memory rate limiting with per-IP tracking
Cleanup interval to prevent memory leaks

findings.title: In-Memory Rate Limiting Lost on Server Restart
findings.issue: Rate limiter uses in-memory Map. On server restart, all rate-limit state is lost. Attacker can bypass limits by waiting for restart.
findings.code_snippet: private store: Map<string, RateLimitRecord> = new Map()
findings.impact: Rate limiting effectiveness: 0 immediately after deployment. Must use Redis/distributed store for production.
findings.remediation: Migrate to Redis: INCR key with EXPIRE. Works across server restarts and load balancers.
findings.evidence: InMemoryRateLimitStore class uses ephemeral Map

findings.title: Rate Limiting Doesn't Work With Load Balancers or Multiple Instances
findings.issue: Global limiters Map is process-specific. If app runs on multiple servers, each server has separate rate-limit state. Attacker distributes requests across servers to bypass limits.
findings.code_snippet: const limiters: Map<string, RateLimiter> = new Map()  // Per-process state
findings.impact: HIGH: In distributed systems, rate limiting is ineffective. Attacker can make 5 requests/server = 5x limit if 5 servers.
findings.remediation: Use Redis for distributed rate limiting: redis.INCR('ratelimit:' + ip), redis.EXPIRE()
findings.evidence: limiters Map is not shared across processes

findings.title: IP Detection Fallback May Give Everyone Same Rate Limit if X-Forwarded-For Missing
findings.issue: getClientIp() falls back to 'anonymous' or '0.0.0.0' if no X-Forwarded-For header. If reverse proxy doesn't set this header, all requests share same rate limit bucket.
findings.code_snippet: // getClientIp() fallback unclear - if all requests get same bucket, DDoS
findings.impact: If misconfigured proxy, attacker can DDoS entire service using single IP rate-limit bucket
findings.remediation: Verify proxy sets X-Forwarded-For. Fallback to request.socket.remoteAddress, not 'anonymous'
findings.evidence: Need to review getClientIp() implementation

findings.title: No Distributed Rate Limiting Across API Gateway / Load Balancer
findings.issue: Rate limiting happens at application level, not at API gateway level. Attacker can still overload infrastructure before reaching application.
findings.code_snippet: // Rate limiting is app-level, not infrastructure-level
findings.impact: DDoS protection is incomplete. Network infrastructure and gateway can still be overwhelmed.
findings.remediation: Add API Gateway rate limiting (Cloudflare, nginx, AWS API Gateway) BEFORE traffic reaches app
findings.evidence: No mention of gateway-level rate limiting
